about.title: Santa Rosa Medical Malpractice Claims
about.longDescription: Medical care in Santa Rosa is supposed to make things better. When it doesn't, the question that keeps people up at night is whether something actually went wrong or whether it was simply a hard case. California law draws that line clearly: a poor result by itself is not malpractice. What matters is whether a doctor, nurse, or facility in Sonoma County fell below the accepted standard of care and that lapse caused harm. Proving it almost always takes a qualified medical expert who can explain what should have happened instead. Timing is tight, too. Under MICRA, most claims must be filed within one year of discovering the injury and never more than three years from when it occurred, with a 90-day notice sent before suit. LawProactive is not a law firm. We are a free service that connects Santa Rosa residents with an independent attorney who handles these cases on contingency, so there is no fee unless there is a recovery. If you're unsure whether your experience counts, asking costs nothing.

items.question: How do I know if what happened to me was malpractice or just bad luck?
items.answer: Medicine involves risk, and an unwanted outcome on its own is not malpractice under California law. The test is whether the provider did something a reasonably careful professional would not have done, and whether that choice caused your harm. A qualified medical expert is nearly always needed to answer that question. An independent attorney can arrange that review at no upfront cost.

items.question: I was injured in a crash on US-101 near Santa Rosa and then my treatment made things worse. Do I have one claim or two?
items.answer: Possibly two. The collision itself may support a personal injury claim against the at-fault driver, while a later error in your care could be a separate malpractice claim. With 790 people injured on Santa Rosa roads in 2025, this overlap comes up more than you might expect. An attorney can sort out how the two interact and which deadlines apply to each.

items.question: How long do I have to file a medical malpractice case in Sonoma County?
items.answer: Under MICRA, you generally have one year from the date you discovered, or reasonably should have discovered, the injury, and never more than three years from when it occurred. Before filing, a 90-day notice must be sent to the provider. Because the discovery date can be disputed, it helps to speak with an attorney sooner rather than later.
